performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
intro: The Elegia, marked Andante non troppo, is the central slow movement of the Concerto for Orchestra, Sz. 116. It begins with a low line in the strings while flute and clarinet play runs above it, and after the loud climaxes the movement closes with the piccolo.

sections.label: Intro · Low strings and woodwind figures
sections.mNote: Double basses begin; woodwinds play figures above held string notes.

sections.label: A · Piccolo calls and trumpet lament
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases lead to a lament for full orchestra.

sections.label: Link · Held horn chord, pizzicato cellos
sections.mNote: Solo cellos play pizzicato beneath a held horn chord.

sections.label: B · Viola melody, muted violins, harps
sections.mNote: Viola melody against short figures in violins and harps.

sections.label: C · High chords over moving lower strings
sections.mNote: Flutes and violins play chords above the moving lower parts.

sections.label: Coda · Low strings, flute and clarinet
sections.mNote: The opening string phrase returns beneath flute and clarinet runs.

cues.title: Opening, double basses
cues.text: The double basses begin, with timpani beside them. Cellos, violas and second violins enter in turn. The phrase repeats the slow ascent from the bottom of the orchestra that opens the first movement.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, plate B. & H. 9009, p. 47, opening bars; compare the fourth-based low-string phrase on p. 1: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eleven-note groups, flute and clarinet
cues.text: In bars 10–17 the flute and clarinet play rising and falling groups of eleven notes. The harp adds glissandos, and the oboe holds a long sustained line. The strings sustain beneath them.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 47–50, bars 10–17: eleven-note flute and clarinet groups, harp glissandos, sustained oboe and strings: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bartók’s note for the Boston première, 1944
cues.text: In his note for the Boston première Bartók called this movement a “lugubrious death-song”. He described the concerto as moving from the sternness of the first movement and this death-song to the life-assertion of the last.
cues.evidence: Bartók’s note for the Boston première (1944), quoted in Richard Rodda’s Pittsburgh Symphony programme note, https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf, and at https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto.

cues.title: Saranac Lake, 1943
cues.text: In 1943 Bartók worked on the concerto at Saranac Lake in upstate New York while recovering from illness. Koussevitzky’s commission had reached him in hospital. By autumn the five movements were finished.
cues.evidence: Richard E. Rodda, Pittsburgh Symphony programme, January 2020, on Koussevitzky’s hospital visit and the Saranac Lake stay: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. Composition dates, 15 August–8 October 1943: https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto

cues.title: Solo cellos, pizzicato
cues.text: A sharp horn chord is followed by a long, quiet note. Below wavering oboes and clarinets, two solo cellos play quick pizzicato figures. The violins and violas play close to the bridge, and the tam-tam sounds softly behind them.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 58–59, bars 54–61: horns, paired woodwinds, two solo pizzicato cello parts, sul ponticello upper strings and tam-tam: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Viola melody, bar 62
cues.text: From bar 62 the violas play a legato line marked molto espressivo, legato. Bartók also writes molto rubato, so the phrase may move freely against the beat. Muted violins and two harps play shorter figures.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 59–60, from bar 62: Poco agitato, mosso, molto rubato; viola melody and its accompaniment: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bartók’s complaint, end of 1942
cues.text: At the end of 1942 Bartók complained: “The quasi boycott of my works by the leading orchestras continues; no performances either of old works or new ones.” Within months Koussevitzky’s commission reached him in hospital.
cues.evidence: Bartók at the end of 1942, quoted in Richard Rodda’s Pittsburgh Symphony programme note, with the commission in 1943: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf

cues.title: High chords over moving lower parts
cues.text: Flutes and violins play repeated high chords. Below them, the clarinets, bassoons, violas and cellos move in continuous lines.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 62–64, especially the repeated chords and moving lower parts from bar 86: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening phrase
cues.text: At bar 99 (Tempo I) the opening phrase returns in basses, cellos and violas. The flute and clarinet runs return above it. The muted horn holds a single note beneath them.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 65–66, bars 99–111: return of the low-string phrase, Tempo I, woodwind runs and muted horn: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Reiner in Pittsburgh, 1946
cues.text: Fritz Reiner conducted the Concerto in Pittsburgh on 18 and 20 January 1946 and recorded it on 4–5 February. Bartók had died on 26 September 1945.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz, Comments to the Henle edition, sources CR and RecR (performances of 18 and 20 January 1946; recording of 4–5 February): https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf. Bartók’s death on 26 September 1945: Rodda, Pittsburgh Symphony programme note, https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf

cues.title: Closing bars, piccolo and timpani
cues.text: The piccolo plays short calls above a muted horn and the last notes of the strings. When the strings stop, piccolo and timpani play the ending pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 67, bars 118–128: piccolo, muted horn, string withdrawal and quiet timpani close: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Wind runs pass to the strings
transitions.from: Intro · Low strings and woodwind figures
transitions.to: A · Piccolo calls and trumpet lament
transitions.how: The flute and clarinet runs spread into several parts. A muted horn holds its note over cellos and violas, and the violas bow close to the bridge. Divided violins take up the winding figures. Piccolo calls and short brass phrases lead to the first full lament.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 51–53, bars 22–34: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Horn chord over plucked cellos
transitions.from: A · Piccolo calls and trumpet lament
transitions.to: Link · Held horn chord, pizzicato cellos
transitions.how: At bar 54 the horns strike a chord and immediately drop to piano. Oboes and clarinets alternate between neighbouring notes. Below them, solo cellos pluck rapid figures; the double basses are silent. The upper strings bow near the bridge, and the tam-tam plays soft strokes behind the held horn chord.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 58–59, bars 54–61: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Móricz discusses the conflicting horn muting and stopping instructions at bar 54: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf

transitions.title: Viola entry at Poco agitato
transitions.from: Link · Held horn chord, pizzicato cellos
transitions.to: B · Viola melody, muted violins, harps
transitions.how: The wind oscillations broaden and stop. A few pizzicato notes in the cellos and basses lead to the viola entry, marked molto espressivo, legato. Bartók marks the new Poco agitato phrase molto rubato. Muted violins and the two harps follow the violas.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 59–60, bars 60–66: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: High chords over the rising line
transitions.from: B · Viola melody, muted violins, harps
transitions.to: C · High chords over moving lower strings
transitions.how: At Tempo I, cor anglais and clarinets begin a rising line, and the bassoons join them. From bar 86, high chords in the flutes and violins cut across this line. Violas and cellos carry on with the lower melody while the upper parts repeat their accented chords.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 62–64, Tempo I and the chords from bar 86: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The low-string phrase returns
transitions.from: C · High chords over moving lower strings
transitions.to: Coda · Low strings, flute and clarinet
transitions.how: The outburst dies down to flute and clarinet runs over a violin note that fades. Low strings play the opening phrase again, marked piano. At Tempo I the woodwind runs resume above held strings and a muted horn, with quiet timpani underneath.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 65–66, bars 99–111: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, III
source.locator: Boosey & Hawkes full score, printed pp. 47–67: low strings, wind runs, the viola lament and the final piccolo calls.

timeline.note: Double basses begin beside quiet timpani; cellos, violas and second violins enter in turn (p. 47).
Flute and clarinet play runs around the oboe’s long line, over strings and harp (pp. 47–50).
Short wind phrases, brass chords and divided strings join the lament (pp. 53–55).
The violas play an expressive line, answered by muted violins and two harps (pp. 59–60).
Cor anglais begins a line that spreads through the lower parts beneath high flute and violin chords (pp. 62–64).
Flutes and clarinets run over held strings and a muted horn (pp. 65–66).
Piccolo calls sound above a muted horn and fading strings, with a few notes from the timpani and harp (p. 67).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: Composer who saw a future for concert music in village songs and used a phonograph to record how they were sung.
facts: István Thomán, a Liszt pupil, and Hans Koessler; Budapest Academy, 1899–1903
Piano professor in Budapest, 1907–34; folk-music research in Budapest and at Columbia University
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages; Biskra, 1913; Turkey with Adnan Saygun, 1936
Six quartets, three piano concertos, two violin concertos, three stage works and Mikrokosmos
composer.background:
In May 1904 Bartók went to stay with the Fischer family at Gerlicepuszta. He had a piano sent out, practised four hours a day and composed for four or five more. There he heard Lidi Dósa, a young woman from Transylvania in the family’s service, singing to the children in her care, and began writing down her songs. Their Hungarian music differed from the urban entertainment that usually went by that name, and he wanted more of it. Two years later the writer Béla Balázs went collecting with Bartók and recorded in his diary that the frail-looking pianist wore him out: “I was already very tired, but he kept urging and driving me on to collect more!”

Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós in 1881, when the town belonged to Hungary; it is now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. His father, director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven. His mother Paula supported Béla and his sister by teaching, moving between towns before settling in Pozsony, now Bratislava. At the Budapest Academy he studied piano with István Thomán, who had studied with Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler.
